task: Write a 350–500-word orientation article for newcomers to a fictional skill-sharing circle. The reader thinks joining requires repaying the same person with an equivalent lesson. Explain network reciprocity, walk through a first introduction and meeting, and clarify boundaries and what happens when a match is not right. Use the supplied illustration as an illustration, not a reported success story. Develop the useful general explanation without turning it into a recruitment pitch, a contract, or a promise of professional expertise.

facts.text: Swap Circle members list skills they can share and things they would like help learning.
A member who receives help need not repay the same person.
Members may instead help someone else in the circle.
The circle does not keep hour balances or monetary accounts.
The coordinator introduces potential matches.
Members agree on their own meeting arrangements.
The coordinator does not certify members' qualifications.
Offers may concern practical, creative, or organising skills.
The coordinator's illustrative example is a member receiving help with paper folding and later helping a different member rehearse a short talk; it is not a reported exchange outcome.
A newcomer may join to learn even if they have nothing to offer immediately.
Joining the circle is free.
The coordinator shares contact details for an introduction only after both people agree.
Before suggesting a match, the coordinator asks what the learner hopes to do and what the other member is offering.
The circle suggests a 20-minute introductory conversation before arranging a full learning session.
The two members should agree the place, time, and needed materials before meeting.
Any material expenses must be agreed beforehand, and the circle does not automatically reimburse them.
Either person may stop an exchange without creating an hour debt.
A member may decline an introduction without giving a reason.
Agreeing to one activity does not commit a member to continuing help.
A member may ask the coordinator for a different introduction if a proposed match is not suitable.
The coordinator may pause further introductions while a conduct concern is reviewed.
The circle's participation rules prohibit exchanges of passwords, financial-account access, or house keys.
Clinical advice, legal representation, and licensed-trade jobs are outside the circle's activities.
The circle does not guarantee that a requested match will be available.
Members can update or remove their offers through the coordinator.

forbidden_additions: Mandatory direct repayment, equal-hour exchanges, or a points balance.
Verified professional qualifications or guaranteed teaching quality.
Coordinator-set appointments, an unprovided fee, or a contractual service guarantee.
The illustrative exchange presented as a verified participant result.
Automatic sharing of contact details, obligatory continuing help, or automatic reimbursement.
Permission to share account access or use the circle for the excluded professional services.
preserve: Reciprocity across the group rather than a one-to-one debt.
Introductions distinguished from certification and scheduling.
A useful explanation for a newcomer without promotional exaggeration.
The practical first-meeting sequence and each member's ability to decline or stop.
The distinction between peer help, professional credentials, and a guaranteed match.
An orientation article with substantive process and boundaries rather than repeated generic reassurance.
